title: Savitri
hook: the warning was spoken at her father's court, and in the forest, only Savitri carries it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri, the princess named for the goddess who rose out of her father's fire, and for the verse he offered with. Did you hear the story behind someone's name? Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

The warning was spoken once, in a palace. When the sage Narada said that Satyavan would die within the year, he said it at a royal court, to Savitri and her father. Then the wedding happened in a forest hermitage, far from that court. Satyavan didn't hear the warning. His parents didn't hear it. The hermits didn't hear it. So Savitri moves into her new home carrying a sentence about her husband that nobody around her has heard. Today is about what she does with it, and what she doesn't say.
screen: `WHO ELSE KNEW?` → `THE WARNING STAYED AT COURT.` → `SHE CARRIES IT ALONE.`

segments.voice: Look first at what the epic says she does. She takes off her jewels and wears the rough cloth of the forest. She looks after her husband's parents, an old king who has lost his sight and his kingdom, and his wife. She is gentle with everyone. And through all of it, the epic says, Narada's words stay in her mind, day and night. She is counting. Now look at what she doesn't do. She doesn't tell Satyavan. She doesn't tell his parents. When the day draws near and she takes a hard vow, fasting and standing through three nights, her father-in-law worries it's too much for her. She doesn't explain. She just tells him gently that she will finish it. On the last morning, when Satyavan picks up his axe for the forest, she asks to go along. He's surprised. She asks his parents' leave, and they give it. Nobody hears a lie from her. Nobody hears the reason, either. Here the epic goes quiet in an interesting way: it never tells us why she keeps the secret. Some readers hear mercy in it, sparing the people she loves a year of dread. Some hear resolve: telling would turn her vow into everyone's grief. Some just notice how heavy it must have been. The text leaves room for all of them. What it does show clearly is that her silence isn't the silence of someone hiding from the truth. She looks at it every day. She counts toward it. She gets ready for it with her own body. A secret can be a way of running. Hers is a way of staying awake.
screen: `SHE SERVES AND SHE COUNTS` · `SHE TELLS NO ONE WHY` · `THE EPIC NEVER SAYS WHY` · `A SILENCE THAT STAYS AWAKE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let something you're carrying sit beside you. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one thing you know that the people around you don't, a worry, a piece of news, a weight. You don't have to solve it or decide whether to tell anyone. Just let it sit next to you, the way you'd let a friend sit beside you on a bench. Breathe with it there. Notice that you're still breathing, still here. If you pray, you can hold it in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Savitri. The young wife who heard a hard truth at her father's court, carried it alone into the forest, and never looked away from it. Today's word.
Your line: Savitri. Today, be gentle with someone who might be carrying something you can't see. You don't have to know what it is. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Hindus hear Savitri's story in the Mahabharata's forest book, where the sage Markandeya tells it to Yudhishthira; it is retold in homes and temples, often around the vow some married women keep in her name.

original.note: Sanskrit: the princess's name, the same as the goddess who gave her and the verse to the sun god Savitr.

notes: Year 3 day 797 covered the hermitage and the three-night vow as plot; this day turns on her silence and the epic's own silence about why. Confirm the epic indeed gives no stated reason for her not telling Satyavan or his parents.
'Three nights' is from the epic's triratra vow; confirm.
'Nobody hears a lie from her': confirm she gives no false reason when asking to go into the forest (she says she wants to go with him and cannot bear to stay behind).
